items.title: The Great Storm of October 1987
items.summary: A deep Atlantic depression crossed southern England during the night of 15–16 October 1987, bringing destructive winds to England and northern France. The Met Office counts 18 deaths directly caused by the storm in England. About 15 million trees were blown down, and at the peak 3 million homes and businesses were without electricity. Gusts reached 98 knots at Shoreham-by-Sea and at least 216 km/h on the Normandy coast.

impacts.text: The Met Office counts 18 direct storm deaths in England. This excludes deaths in other countries.

The Forestry Commission estimated 15 million fallen trees, representing 3.9 million cubic metres of timber. It reported 3 million householders and businesses without electricity at the peak of the cuts, and no Southern Region trains running on the morning of 16 October.
Buildings and boats were damaged. Fallen trees blocked transport and broke power lines. Gatwick Airport closed.

history.text: Later forecasts shifted the main threat south. Evening broadcasts emphasised rain and missed the exceptional winds. Michael Fish denied that a hurricane was coming; the Met Office says he meant another Atlantic system.
Emergency authorities received warnings, and the Ministry of Defence was alerted at 0135 UTC on 16 October.

Afterwards, more ocean buoys were deployed to watch the seas south-west of the British Isles, and the Met Office set up the National Severe Weather Warning Service to warn emergency services and the public.

why_interesting.text: The low deepened by 17 hPa in 12 hours as it crossed the Bay of Biscay. The pressure rises behind it were exceptional: 12 hPa in one hour at Hurn, near Bournemouth.
Its track took it from west of Spain to north-west of Brittany by 00 GMT 16 Oct, over Exeter at 02 GMT and to Hull around 05–06 GMT. The most damaging winds lay south and south-east of the track.
It became a key case for the sting jet: air descending from the cloud head near its hooked tip, bringing the damaging winds seen in the dry slot.
Some records were revised. The Met Office later reduced Gorleston's 106 knots to 85 knots because the anemometer cups were bent, leaving Shoreham as the strongest measured gust in England.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 reaches 951 hPa off Brittany at 22 UTC 15 Oct, close to published central-pressure analyses of 952–953 hPa around 00 GMT 16 Oct. Its peak gusts at Shoreham are 40 m/s during 03–04 UTC 16 Oct and at Pointe du Roc 35 m/s during 00–01 UTC 16 Oct, below the station evidence. The largest shortfall is at Pointe du Roc, where the recorder reached 60 m/s, so the actual peak remains uncertain. These differences likely reflect the coarse representation of coastlines, exposed headlands and small wind features; London’s rooftop instrument also differs from a standard surface wind measurement.

items.title: Hurricane Katrina

where.label: Gulf of Mexico, south-east Louisiana and coastal Mississippi

items.summary: Katrina rapidly strengthened over the Gulf of Mexico on 26-28 August 2005, reaching Category 5 with a central pressure of 902 hPa and maximum sustained winds of 150 knots. It weakened to Category 3 before landfalls near Buras, Louisiana, and the Louisiana-Mississippi border on 29 August, but its broad wind field drove a large storm surge onto the Mississippi coast. Surge and failures of levees and floodwalls flooded about 80% of New Orleans. The National Hurricane Center's revised US toll is 1,392 deaths, including direct, indirect and indeterminate causes, with total damage estimated at US$125 billion in 2005 dollars.

impacts.text: The National Hurricane Center's 2023 revision counts 1,392 deaths in the United States: 520 direct, 565 indirect and 307 with an indeterminate cause. These are whole-event figures, including deaths outside Louisiana and Mississippi. Earlier counts used different information: the 2006 NWS assessment provisionally listed 1,353 direct deaths, while early NHC reports put all deaths above 1,800.

Storm surge and waves destroyed homes, businesses and public buildings along the Mississippi coast. In New Orleans, overtopping and breaches of levees and floodwalls flooded about 80% of the city, with water reaching about 20 feet in places. Wind damaged buildings and power lines, and floods and destroyed bridges disrupted transport across the northern Gulf coast.

The updated National Hurricane Center report gives total US damage of US$125 billion in 2005 dollars, using NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information estimates. This is total damage, rather than insured loss alone. Flooded refineries, damaged offshore platforms and disrupted workplaces added to the storm's economic effects.

history.text: The NWS review found that NHC had forecast a major hurricane affecting the central Gulf coast, including New Orleans, about 56 hours before landfall. A hurricane watch covered south-east Louisiana from 10 a.m. CDT on 27 August; a warning followed that evening. At 10:11 a.m. CDT on 28 August, the New Orleans/Baton Rouge office issued its detailed bulletin on devastating damage and prolonged uninhabitable conditions. The review says broadcasters and emergency managers used its impact wording to prepare the public.

The post-event NWS assessment called for more resilient power and communications, stronger arrangements for offices backing each other up, and a separate code and standard wording for destructive hurricane wind warnings. These were recommendations following failures of infrastructure and confusion over warning formats during Katrina.

In 2017, NWS and NHC introduced separate operational storm surge watches and warnings for the continental US Gulf and Atlantic coasts. These distinguished the danger from rising coastal water from the wind hazard; the two can affect different places at different times.

why_interesting.text: Over the Gulf, a large anticyclone aloft gave Katrina weak wind shear and efficient outflow, allowing thunderstorms to organise around its centre. The ridge that had steered it west shifted towards Florida while a trough grew over the north-central United States. Katrina then curved north-west and north towards the Gulf coast.

Katrina underwent two periods of rapid intensification on 26-28 August. During the second, its central pressure fell by 32 hPa in the 12 hours ending at 12 UTC 28 Aug. Aircraft observations supported a minimum pressure of 902 hPa and an estimated maximum sustained surface wind of 150 knots at 18 UTC 28 Aug over the central Gulf.

Changes in the rings of thunderstorms around the eye helped Katrina weaken before landfall, while its wind field remained broad. NHC estimates sustained winds of 110 knots near Buras at 11:10 UTC 29 Aug and 105 knots at the Pearl River mouth at 14:45 UTC 29 Aug, both Category 3. Post-storm analysis reduced the Buras estimate from 120 to 110 knots because the winds aloft were not reaching the surface as efficiently as the usual adjustment assumed.

The weakening wind category did not remove the surge hazard. Katrina's broad onshore winds pushed water towards Mississippi, while waves generated during its stronger offshore phase raised water levels further. FEMA high-water-mark surveys put surge at about 24-28 feet along the coast around St Louis Bay, including a 27.8-foot mark at Pass Christian. This was a surveyed mark left by the water, rather than a continuously recorded peak.

Rising water in Lake Pontchartrain and the canals strained New Orleans' flood defences. Many breaches followed overtopping and erosion, but some floodwalls failed before water reached their tops. Heavy rain accompanied the hurricane, but the city's inundation cannot be explained as rainfall flooding alone.

The strongest gust at an official reporting station was 99 knots at Grand Isle C-MAN at 08:38 UTC 29 Aug; larger unofficial gusts were also reported. Rain was heaviest along and just west of the storm's track across south-east Louisiana and south-west Mississippi. The Slidell NWS office measured a storm total of 11.63 inches, about 295 mm.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows Katrina from the eastern Gulf on 27 August to south-east Louisiana on 29 August, but its minimum is 932 hPa south of Buras at 10 UTC 29 Aug, much later and less deep than the observed 902 hPa offshore at 18 UTC 28 Aug. At the observed peak hour it gives 952 hPa over the central Gulf, so the apparently closer landfall pressure does not mean it captures the earlier intensity; smoothing of the small eye and eyewall is a likely contributor. Grand Isle's maximum hourly gust is 48 m/s at 10 UTC 29 Aug, while New Orleans Lakefront's is 49 m/s at 13 UTC 29 Aug; the station instruments failed before the full wind event was sampled, and their brief gusts and differing exposure are not identical to an hourly model maximum. Slidell has 211 mm for the 48 hours ending 12 UTC 30 Aug against a measured storm total of about 295 mm, whose exact gauge reporting times are not stated, so the rain comparison is approximate; these atmospheric maps do not reconstruct storm surge, levee failure or flood depth.

items.title: Cyclone Gabrielle

where.label: North Island, especially Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay

items.summary: Ex-tropical Cyclone Gabrielle brought destructive wind and rain to the North Island on 12–14 February 2023 NZDT, affecting Northland, Auckland and Coromandel first. It slowed near the Coromandel as an upper trough renewed its strength, feeding prolonged rain onto the hills of Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay overnight on 13–14 February NZDT. Mokohinau measured a gust of 150 km/h on 12 February NZDT, while Napier Airport measured 175.8 mm of rain from 9am 13 February to 9am 14 February NZDT. NZHistory records 11 deaths in New Zealand; floods and slips damaged homes, farmland and transport links, and cut power and communications.

impacts.text: NZHistory counts 11 deaths in New Zealand from Gabrielle: eight in Hawke’s Bay, one at Te Karaka inland of Gisborne, and two volunteer firefighters caught in a landslide at Muriwai. Its account identifies deaths from the event rather than a formal direct-versus-indirect classification.

Floodwater reached homes in the Esk Valley and Te Karaka, while slips damaged houses on Auckland’s west coast. Roads were cut, communities lost power and communications, and floodwater and silt damaged orchards, vineyards and other farmland in Hawke’s Bay. A national state of emergency was declared on 14 February NZDT.

The Insurance Council of New Zealand’s February 2025 review puts Gabrielle’s insured losses at about NZ$1.8 billion, with the price basis not stated. This is insured loss alone; the larger Treasury damage range often quoted combines Gabrielle with the Auckland Anniversary floods.

history.text: MetService issued heavy-rain and strong-wind watches on 9 February NZDT, orange warnings on 11 February, and its first red warnings that afternoon. Agreement between forecast models increased its confidence in an impact on New Zealand.

The Government’s October 2024 response to the North Island severe-weather inquiry acknowledged gaps in public warnings. It reported a new arrangement with Radio New Zealand for broadcasts at set times in areas without power, and work with MetService to put civil-defence preparedness advice alongside severe-weather warnings.

why_interesting.text: Gabrielle arrived during a La Niña summer with unusually frequent easterly and north-easterly winds drawing warm, humid air towards New Zealand. Warm surrounding seas increased the moisture available to passing lows. Earlier rain had already left northern districts vulnerable to further flooding and slips.

Losing tropical status did not end the storm’s development. Interaction with the subtropical jet, temperature contrasts and an upper trough from the Tasman Sea renewed Gabrielle’s strength. The trough also slowed and turned the cyclone towards Great Barrier Island and the Coromandel late on 13 February NZDT.

The pause near the northern coast sustained moist winds against the steep hills behind Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay. Uplift wrung rain from that air, and steep slopes carried water rapidly into rivers and low-lying settlements. This links the offshore track to the flooding overnight on 13–14 February NZDT.
The broad circulation spread strong winds across distant regions. Low pressure, onshore gales and swell raised coastal water levels, and storm surge hindered river drainage into the sea.

Napier Airport’s 175.8 mm from 9am 13 February to 9am 14 February NZDT was its wettest February day in records beginning in 1950. NIWA lists a 150 km/h gust measured at Mokohinau on 12 February NZDT. A later modelling study estimated that historical human-caused warming increased regional storm rainfall totals by about 10%.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows the slowdown near the Coromandel, reaching 967 hPa north-east of the peninsula at 15 UTC 13 Feb, before moving east towards East Cape on 14 February. At Napier Airport it gives 144 mm in the 24 hours ending 20 UTC 13 Feb, compared with 175.8 mm measured over the same period. Its peak Mokohinau gust is 31 m/s at 19 UTC 12 Feb, whereas NIWA reports 150 km/h on 12 February NZDT, so both strength and timing differ. The coarse grid smooths steep terrain and exposed sites; local rain and gust extremes, and the river flooding they produced, need finer detail than these weather maps provide.
